title: Choose Life Insurance by Need, Not Pitch
meta_description: Calculate your life-insurance need, compare term and permanent policies, read guarantees, review beneficiaries, and avoid costly replacement mistakes.

module_headings.summary: Summary: Match the Contract to the Financial Need
module_headings.sources: Evidence Notes for Policies, Illustrations and Claims

sections.heading: Start With the People Who Need the Money
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows two parents and two young children at home. It makes the purpose of life insurance visible: replacing financial support when a person dies, so survivors can pay bills, care for dependants and make decisions without an immediate cash crisis.

Insurance is not a verdict on how valuable a life is. It is a contract designed to fund specific consequences. Name the people or organisations exposed, the money they would need, when they would need it and how long the exposure lasts.

Term insurance covers a defined period when conditions are met. Permanent policies, including whole life and forms of universal life, are designed to remain in force longer and may build policy value. Neither label decides suitability without the need, guarantees, costs and alternatives.

Reject slogans in both directions. ‘Always buy term’ ignores durable estate, business or lifelong-dependant needs. ‘You get nothing back from term’ ignores that pure risk transfer is the product, just as a home policy need not return premiums to have worked.
Use a needs analysis before a product illustration. Calculate survivor income, debts, care, education, final expenses, taxes and existing resources. Then match duration and certainty.

This guide is educational, not personal insurance, tax or legal advice. Products, consumer protections, taxation and estate treatment vary by jurisdiction. Verify current documents and use appropriately authorised professionals for consequential decisions.

Create a survivor memo before calculating. Describe what happens in the first week, first year and later years after each adult’s death. Include who provides care, who returns to work, which home is retained and which goals remain. This turns an abstract death-benefit target into decisions that can be costed and discussed respectfully.

Separate emotional urgency from contractual urgency. A new child, diagnosis in the family or alarming sales story can accelerate attention, but it should not remove comparison. Set a short decision timetable, gather records and preserve temporary existing coverage. A deliberate process can move quickly without pretending that the first quotation is the only chance to protect the household.

Ask each adult privately whether the plan reflects their expectations about work, care and housing. Hidden disagreement about a survivor returning to work can change the need far more than a minor premium difference.

sections.heading: Calculate the Gap, Not a Round Number
paragraphs: List immediate cash needs: funeral and administration, medical bills, debts due, emergency liquidity and professional help. Avoid automatically adding every debt if survivors would sell the associated asset.

Model ongoing household spending after death. Some costs fall, while childcare, transport, health coverage or household services may rise. Use actual spending and discuss the daily work each adult performs without pay.
Estimate survivor income from work, pensions, public benefits, rentals and existing insurance. Apply conservative timing and eligibility rather than counting a benefit that has not been confirmed.

Set goals separately. Education, mortgage payoff, support for parents, charitable gifts and inheritance are different obligations. A goal can be reduced or delayed; essential care may not be flexible.

Subtract liquid assets intended for survivors, but do not count the emergency fund twice or assume retirement assets are accessible without tax and timing costs. Preserve assets needed by the surviving spouse for their own old age.
The result is a range, not a magic multiple of salary. Show a base case and a difficult case with longer care, slower income recovery or inflation.

Value unpaid household work explicitly. Childcare, eldercare, transport, cooking and administration may need paid replacement or reduced survivor work. A person with little employment income can still create a large insurance need. Conversely, high earnings do not automatically justify enormous coverage if assets and obligations already protect survivors.

Model household income month by month for the first two years. Survivor benefits, salary changes, childcare and claim payment may start on different dates. Include a liquidity bridge even when long-term assets are sufficient. Selling investments or a home during grief can lock in poor timing; accessible proceeds can buy decision space rather than permanently increasing lifestyle.

Document every resource with owner, amount, tax status, access time and intended use. A jointly discussed asset is not automatically available to a beneficiary, and an illiquid business interest cannot pay next month’s bills.

sections.heading: Match the Coverage Term to the Liability
paragraphs: Draw a timeline from today through the last material obligation. Mortgage, dependent children, a nonworking spouse’s transition, business debt and education can end on different dates.

A level term can cover a broad peak period. Layered terms can reduce total coverage as obligations decline, but multiple policies add administration and underwriting risk when replacing an expiring layer.
Do not choose a short term merely to obtain the lowest displayed premium. Requalifying later may be expensive or impossible after a health change.
A renewable or convertible provision can add flexibility. Read the deadline, eligible products, maximum age and pricing basis; ‘convertible’ does not mean conversion will be cheap.
Coverage through work is useful but can be tied to employment and may be insufficient or nonportable. Verify conversion and portability windows before leaving a job.
Review the timeline after births, divorce, debt changes, business obligations and retirement. A policy should change because the need changed, not because a salesperson found a new product.

Stress the duration as well as amount. A ten-year need and a thirty-year need should not be priced as though equal. Mark uncertainty in education timing, mortgage plans and dependent support. When liabilities overlap, show the peak and decline rather than one permanent block assumed to last forever.

Consider inflation explicitly. A fixed death benefit loses purchasing power over a long term, while debts may amortise and investments may grow. Use a range rather than assuming each cancels perfectly. If staged coverage is used, document which policy addresses which years so an expiring layer does not disappear unnoticed while the liability remains.

If layered terms are used, keep one coverage calendar showing issue, expiry, conversion deadline and purpose. Review the calendar before each layer ends, while health and alternatives can still be assessed deliberately.

sections.heading: Understand What Term Insurance Guarantees
paragraphs: Term insurance generally promises a death benefit during the covered term if the policy is in force and claim conditions are met. Premiums may be level for a period and then rise sharply, or follow another schedule.
Read the guaranteed premium schedule rather than the first-year quote. Confirm term length, death benefit, renewal ages, conversion, exclusions, riders and grace period.
Return-of-premium term is not free reimbursement. Compare its higher premium and conditions with ordinary term plus separately saved money.

A low quote can change after underwriting. The application class, medical evidence, occupation, travel and habits can affect the final offer. Do not cancel existing coverage before new coverage is issued, accepted and effective.
Term often fits large temporary needs because it separates insurance from saving and can provide more death benefit per initial premium. That is an economic tendency, not a universal command.
Ask what happens at the end. The plan may be to self-insure through accumulated assets, retain a smaller converted policy or continue coverage at then-current cost.

Confirm the insurer’s definition of in force, payment due and grace period. Keep beneficiary contact details separate from premium access. If a bank account closes, update instructions with enough time for processing. A contract can provide strong guarantees yet fail because routine administration was neglected.

Compare insurer strength, service and contract—not premium alone. Financial-strength ratings are opinions from separate organisations, use different scales and can change. Check the licensed legal entity issuing the policy, complaint resources and guaranty protections applicable locally. Do not imply that a rating or guaranty association eliminates insurer risk or substitutes for suitable coverage.

Request a specimen contract before applying when possible. Marketing summaries describe features; the issued contract defines rights. Compare definitions and schedules instead of relying on a product name shared by materially different insurer designs.

sections.heading: Permanent Insurance Solves Different Problems
paragraphs: Permanent insurance aims to cover death whenever it occurs if required premiums and policy conditions are maintained. Whole life typically includes guarantees defined in the contract; universal life offers adjustable elements with different guarantee and funding structures.

Possible use cases include liquidity for estate costs, equalising inheritances, funding a buy-sell agreement, supporting a lifelong dependant or providing a deliberately permanent charitable gift. Each requires legal and tax coordination.
A desire to leave ‘something’ is not enough to skip comparison. State the amount, timing, priority and what investment or savings alternatives could provide.
Premiums can be much higher than term. Affordability must survive job loss, retirement and other goals. A lapse after years of payment can be especially damaging.

Cash value is policy property governed by contract. Access through withdrawals or loans can reduce death benefit, create interest and produce tax consequences, especially if the policy lapses with a loan.
Treat permanent insurance as a long-duration contract requiring stress tests, not as a savings account with a free death benefit.

Permanent coverage can also be overfunded or underfunded relative to its design. Ask which elements are contractually required, which are planned and what happens if premiums stop. A policy designed around favourable assumptions may require later payments. Make that possibility visible before it competes with retirement income.

Permanent-policy comparisons should include a low-premium stress case, a missed-payment case and retirement cash flow. Ask whether the design relies on continuous maximum funding, dividends or favourable crediting. If the household cannot explain how the guarantee is maintained, reduce complexity or obtain independent review. Long duration magnifies small misunderstandings in charges, loans and benefit options.

Decide whether liquidity, guarantee, inheritance or living access is the priority. Permanent policies can combine features, but combining them may obscure which objective drives cost. Rank objectives before comparing product variations.

sections.heading: Read the Illustration Without Treating It as a Forecast
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a couple reviewing documents with a professional. That is the right placement for policy illustrations: values must be read line by line, with guarantees separated from assumptions.

Locate guaranteed premium, guaranteed death benefit and guaranteed value. Then identify nonguaranteed dividends, crediting rates, charges or market assumptions. A column on paper is not a promise merely because it contains precise numbers.
Ask for lower-assumption scenarios and a current in-force ledger for an existing policy. Determine what premium is required to keep coverage to the target age under each scenario.

For universal life, understand the guarantee period, cost-of-insurance charges, interest crediting, caps or floors and what happens when value is insufficient. Different universal-life designs carry different risks.
Variable life and variable universal life expose values to investment performance and securities rules. The [[S3|SEC’s variable-life overview]] emphasises fees, investment risk and prospectus review.
Do not compare term death benefit with a permanent policy’s cash value as though they are identical outputs. Compare complete strategies at the same need, time horizon, cash flow and risk.

Request the complete illustration and signed ledger, not selected pages. Check issue age, rating, premium mode and benefit option. Ask the adviser to mark every nonguaranteed number. If the explanation cannot survive plain-language notes, postpone the purchase rather than relying on memory of a verbal presentation.

Illustrations can change through death-benefit options, premium timing and withdrawals, so compare like with like. Confirm whether benefit is level, increasing or includes value in addition to face amount. Ask why each assumption was chosen and whether it complies with current illustration standards. Save the signed illustration actually used, not a later marketing summary with different inputs.

Ask the adviser to explain the illustration without pointing to a sales headline. You should be able to restate premium duty, guarantee duration, downside and surrender result in plain language before accepting the contract.

sections.heading: Price the Whole Strategy
paragraphs: Compare premiums over the period you realistically expect to maintain coverage. Include rider charges, policy fees, investment expenses and adviser compensation where disclosed.

For term plus investing, specify the actual investment account, tax treatment, fees, contribution discipline and return range. ‘Invest the difference’ is not a strategy if the difference will be spent.
For permanent insurance, separate guaranteed and nonguaranteed internal results. Calculate surrender value and death benefit at several dates, not one favourable endpoint.
Use present value cautiously and show assumptions. A single internal rate of return can hide liquidity limits, lapse risk and the fact that death timing is unknown.
Include the value of flexibility. Term can be cancelled easily but may be hard to replace. Permanent insurance can preserve insurability but may demand long funding.

The lower expected-cost strategy can still be wrong if it fails the required certainty; the higher-guarantee strategy can be wrong if premiums crowd out emergency savings, retirement or essential coverage.

Compare strategies at multiple death dates and at survival dates when coverage might be surrendered. Include the household’s likely behaviour: saving discipline, risk tolerance and access needs. An elegant spreadsheet that assumes perfect investing or uninterrupted premiums can mislead more than a simple conservative comparison.

Build an affordability ratio that shows premium alongside emergency saving, retirement contributions, debt payments and essential insurance. Test it after a pay cut and at retirement. Coverage that lapses because it consumed too much cash never delivered its intended certainty. A smaller sustainable design can protect more effectively than a large policy maintained only under perfect income.

Keep assumptions consistent across proposals: insured health class, benefit, payment schedule, duration and tax view. Comparisons using different inputs can create an apparent advantage that comes from the setup rather than the policy.

sections.heading: Underwriting Is Part of the Purchase
paragraphs: Answer application questions completely and accurately. Material misstatements can threaten a claim, particularly during a contestability period. Ask for clarification rather than guessing.
Understand accelerated, simplified and guaranteed-issue routes. Less underwriting can mean lower available coverage, higher cost or graded benefits. Convenience is not the only dimension.
Timing matters, but urgency should not override disclosure. Gather medical, prescription, financial and travel information before applying.

Work with an authorised producer who can explain which insurers were considered and why. Verify licence or registration independently; the [[S6|FCA Firm Checker]] is one UK route, while U.S. buyers can use state insurance-department tools.
Ask how the professional is paid, whether compensation varies by product, and what ongoing service is included. A conflict does not prove bad advice, but it must be visible.
Keep the application, final offer, policy and payment evidence. Compare the issued policy with the proposal before the free-look or cancellation period ends.

Underwriting privacy matters. Submit sensitive information through insurer-approved secure channels and ask how records are used. Do not send medical histories through casual messaging. If an application is postponed, rated or declined, understand what may be recorded before immediately submitting numerous new applications.

If health changes while an application is pending, follow application and insurer disclosure requirements. Do not conceal new information or rely on an intermediary’s casual assurance. Confirm delivery requirements, first premium, effective date and any statement of continued good health. Policy issuance, delivery and coverage commencement are not always the same moment.

Review prescription and medical records for accuracy where lawful and available. Correct errors through proper channels rather than coaching answers. Underwriting should reflect truthful facts, not a strategy for guessing what the insurer prefers.

sections.heading: Riders Should Solve a Named Risk
paragraphs: A rider modifies coverage. Common examples address waiver of premium, accelerated death benefits, children, accidental death or future purchase options. Names and definitions vary.
For each rider, write the event, benefit, exclusions, cost, waiting period and overlap with health, disability or other insurance. Delete riders that lack a defined job.
Accidental-death coverage is narrower than life coverage and should not substitute for an all-cause need. Read how accident and excluded events are defined.
Accelerated benefits can reduce the amount later paid to beneficiaries and may have eligibility, fee and tax implications. They are not identical to comprehensive long-term-care insurance.
A child rider can provide limited coverage and sometimes conversion, but the financial need should be stated sensitively and accurately.
Future-insurability options can matter when health risk or expected need may grow. Confirm exercise dates, limits and whether premiums then use attained age.

Rider marketing often uses emotionally powerful events. Return to probability, overlap and benefit definition. A narrow rider with a dramatic name may pay in fewer circumstances than broader standalone coverage. Ask for claim examples and exclusions, while recognising examples cannot amend the contract.

Riders can expire at different ages or terminate after a claim. Put each rider on the coverage timeline and compare its benefit with a standalone policy. Waiver provisions may define disability differently from workplace coverage. A child rider may cover several children under one amount. Contract wording, not the familiar rider name, controls the result.

Price riders over their actual duration. A small monthly charge can become material over decades, while a valuable option may expire before the expected need. Put dates and cumulative cost beside benefits.

sections.heading: Beneficiaries Make the Contract Operational
paragraphs: Name primary and contingent beneficiaries clearly and keep identifying information current. Avoid relying on a will to override a beneficiary designation where local law gives the policy form priority.
Minor children generally should not receive large proceeds directly without an appropriate legal arrangement. Coordinate guardianship, trusts or custodial rules with qualified legal advice.
Review ownership as well as beneficiary. The insured, owner and payer can be different, affecting control, tax, estate and gift consequences.
Tell a trusted person that coverage exists, the insurer, policy number location and claim contact. Do not place account credentials in an exposed household file.
For business insurance, document valuation, ownership, premium responsibility and buy-sell terms. A policy alone does not create an effective succession agreement.
Review designations after marriage, divorce, birth, death, trust changes and relocation. Outdated forms can defeat the household’s current intention.

Coordinate beneficiary forms with the estate plan and family circumstances. Record why a trust, individual or charity was chosen and who can update it. Where consent or community-property rights may apply, obtain legal guidance. Administrative convenience should not override valid ownership and family-law requirements.

For trusts, identify trustee powers, successor trustees, premium funding and communication with beneficiaries. A trust drafted but never properly connected to policy ownership may not achieve the plan. Insurer forms and legal documents must agree. Review after trustee, residence and family changes; sophisticated paperwork is not self-maintaining merely because it was professionally prepared once.

Beneficiary percentages should total correctly and account for a beneficiary dying first. Use full legal identities and the insurer’s permitted designation language. Ambiguity creates delay precisely when the contract should provide liquidity.

sections.heading: Tax and Estate Claims Need Jurisdiction Labels
paragraphs: Life-insurance tax statements are often oversimplified. In the United States, death proceeds are generally treated differently from interest, transfers for value and policy transactions; [[S7|IRS Publication 525]] gives a federal starting point.

Cash-value growth, withdrawals, loans, surrender and lapse can have different outcomes. Modified endowment contract rules can alter U.S. distributions. Obtain advice before using a policy as an income plan.

In the UK, ownership, trusts and inheritance-tax rules can affect whether proceeds enter an estate and how quickly they reach intended recipients. Use current legal and tax advice rather than a sales diagram.
Cross-border ownership can involve residence, domicile, insurer restrictions, reporting and currency. Inform the insurer before moving and coordinate both jurisdictions.
Do not call benefits tax free without country, tax type and facts. A beneficiary may receive principal differently from interest paid after death.
Preserve tax basis, premium history, loan records and trust documents. Future advisers cannot reconstruct a complex policy reliably from the latest annual statement alone.

Tax planning should not be the first reason for basic family coverage. Establish the protection need, then optimise ownership and funding. Tax laws can change over decades, while an unaffordable contract can lapse much sooner. Date every tax assumption and identify the professional responsible for reviewing it.

Keep claims and tax planning separate. A beneficiary should know the insurer’s process, required documents and options, while an executor or trustee handles estate duties. Interest can accrue if proceeds remain with the insurer and may be treated differently from the death benefit. Compare lump sum and retained-asset options for safety, fees, access and protection before choosing.

For charitable or business designs, obtain written confirmation that the entity can own or receive the policy as planned. Governance, insurable-interest and consent rules can apply before tax treatment is even considered.

sections.heading: Replacing a Policy Creates a Coverage Hazard
paragraphs: Never cancel an existing policy merely because a new illustration looks better. New underwriting, contestability, surrender charges, acquisition costs and loss of guarantees can make replacement harmful.
Compare old and new contracts side by side using current in-force values. Identify what guarantee, conversion right, rating class or rider will be lost.
Ask whether reducing, exchanging, making paid-up, or retaining part of the old policy can meet the goal. Tax rules and insurer procedures require specialist review.
Complete replacement notices accurately. Regulators often impose specific duties because replacements can generate new commissions while resetting important periods.
Do not borrow heavily from an old policy to fund a new one without modelling interest, lapse and tax risk across both contracts.
The burden of proof belongs to the replacement: it should solve a documented problem after all costs and lost rights, not merely display a larger projected column.

Replacement analysis should disclose new commission and surrender impact in currency, not adjectives. Model keeping the old policy, modifying it and replacing it. If the new policy depends on better future performance to recover transaction costs, state the break-even year and what happens if assumptions are lower.

Existing policy values may contain guarantees unavailable today, but age alone does not prove value. Request original contract, amendments, basis, loans, surrender charge and current ledger. If records are missing, obtain them from the insurer before accepting a replacement analysis. Never let a replacement illustration define the old policy through selective or outdated numbers.

Replacement pressure often appears near surrender-charge milestones or after a new product launch. Timing alone is not a reason. Require a written comparison that remains persuasive after commission, tax and lost guarantee are included.

sections.heading: Keep the Policy in Force and Findable
paragraphs: The late photograph shows parents and children reviewing a clipboard with an adviser. It reinforces the operational finish: the family needs understandable records, correct beneficiaries and a policy that remains funded.
Set reliable premium payments and monitor notices. Automatic payment reduces missed bills but does not replace annual review, especially for flexible-premium policies.
Read each annual statement for death benefit, value, loans, charges, credited amounts and lapse projections. Escalate unexplained changes promptly.
Maintain insurer and adviser contacts, policy pages, application, illustration, amendments, statements and trust records in secure storage. Tell the appropriate person how to locate them.
Beneficiaries should know how to start a claim and obtain certified documents without being pressured into unrelated products. Compare payout options rather than accepting one automatically.
Check insurer notices after address, bank or email changes. A policy can fail operationally even when its original design was sound.

Run an annual policy drill. Confirm one trusted person can locate the insurer and policy details, beneficiaries remain correct, payments clear and contact information works. Do not circulate full statements widely. The drill tests access without exposing medical, financial or identity information unnecessarily.

Create a claim-access sheet with insurer legal name, policy number, insured person, owner, beneficiaries, agent or service contact and document location. Exclude passwords and unnecessary medical data. Store one secure copy away from the home where appropriate. Survivors should not need to search emails or recognise a premium debit to discover that protection exists.

Keep premium notices whitelisted and physical mail current, but treat unexpected contact cautiously. Verify through the insurer’s published channel before changing beneficiaries, bank details or ownership in response to an email or call.

sections.heading: Use a Decision Gate Before Signing
paragraphs: Complete the need file: insured person, beneficiaries, amount, duration, purpose, existing resources and difficult-case assumptions.
Complete the contract file: product type, guarantees, nonguaranteed elements, premiums, charges, riders, conversion, lapse conditions and surrender terms.
Complete the adviser file: authorisation check, insurers considered, compensation, conflicts and written recommendation. Refuse pressure tied to an artificial deadline.
Complete the operations file: owner, beneficiaries, contingent beneficiaries, payment, storage, claim contact and annual review date.
Use buy, revise, obtain specialist advice or decline. Specialist advice is especially important for trusts, business succession, cross-border ownership, large estates, policy loans and replacements.

Life insurance works when a real financial loss is transferred for an affordable price under a contract the household can keep and operate. Choose by need, evidence and guarantee—not by a slogan or sales pitch.

Have an independent second reader check the need calculation, dates, guarantee columns, beneficiary names and arithmetic. For a complex policy, pay for advice if appropriate rather than asking only the seller to review their own recommendation. Sign and date the final decision memo and preserve the documents actually relied upon.

Record rejected alternatives and why. The file should show term lengths, permanent designs, coverage amounts and self-insurance options considered. This protects against hindsight and helps future reviews distinguish a changed need from a new sales pitch. If facts change before signing, reopen the gate rather than forcing the old recommendation onto a different household.

Schedule the first review when the policy arrives, the second after the first annual statement and recurring reviews thereafter. Early checks catch issue differences; later checks test whether the need and contract remain aligned.

summary: Life insurance transfers a defined financial loss after death. Start with the people or organisations exposed, what money they need, when they need it and how long the exposure lasts. Insurance amount is not a measure of personal value.

Calculate immediate costs, survivor spending, care, debts and goals, then subtract confirmed income and liquid assets intended for survivors. Include unpaid household work and preserve the survivor’s retirement resources. Use base and difficult cases rather than a salary multiple.

Match coverage duration to obligations. Term insurance generally fits temporary needs efficiently, but renewal and future insurability matter. Permanent insurance can address durable estate, business, charitable or lifelong-dependant needs when affordable and properly coordinated.

Read guarantees separately from assumptions. In permanent and universal-life illustrations, precise nonguaranteed values are not promises. Request lower scenarios and current in-force ledgers. Variable products add market risk, fees and securities disclosures.

Compare complete strategies. For term plus investing, specify the account, fees, tax and actual saving behaviour. For permanent insurance, show premiums, guaranteed and nonguaranteed values, surrender and death outcomes at several dates.

Answer underwriting questions accurately and use secure channels. Verify the professional’s authorisation, insurers considered, compensation and conflicts. Compare the issued policy with the application and proposal during the cancellation period.

Buy riders only for named risks after reviewing event, benefit, exclusions, waiting period, overlap and cost. Accidental death is narrower than all-cause coverage, and accelerated benefits can reduce the later death benefit.

Coordinate owner, insured and beneficiaries. Name contingent beneficiaries, avoid direct large payments to minors without legal planning and align forms with trusts, business agreements and family law. Tell a trusted person how to locate the policy.

Label tax claims by jurisdiction and facts. Death proceeds, interest, withdrawals, loans, surrender and lapse can receive different treatment. Cross-border and trust ownership require coordinated legal and tax advice.

Do not cancel existing coverage before replacement is issued, accepted and effective. Compare old and new guarantees, surrender costs, rating, conversion, contestability and commission. Replacement must solve a documented problem.

Maintain payments, read annual statements and monitor loans, charges and lapse projections. Keep policy, application, illustration, amendments and trust records securely. Beneficiaries should know the claim route without being exposed to unnecessary credentials.

Before signing, complete need, contract, adviser and operations files. Use buy, revise, specialist advice or decline. The right policy transfers a real loss for an affordable premium under a contract the household can understand, maintain and find.

Test affordability after a pay cut and at retirement, not only today. Compare premiums with emergency saving, debt, retirement contributions and other essential protection. A smaller policy maintained reliably can provide more real protection than an elaborate design that depends on uninterrupted high income or optimistic nonguaranteed performance.

Confirm insurer, issuing entity, financial-strength evidence, effective date and first-payment requirements. Keep existing coverage until the replacement is reviewed and active. If health or application facts change before delivery, follow the insurer’s disclosure requirements rather than relying on an informal assurance.

Create a secure claim-access sheet listing insurer, policy, insured person, owner, beneficiaries, service contact and record location without passwords. Run an annual household drill to confirm the policy is findable, payments clear, beneficiaries remain accurate and flexible-premium coverage is not approaching lapse.

Preserve the decision memo, alternatives rejected and documents actually relied upon. When circumstances change, revisit the need instead of accepting a new product automatically. A second reader or independent specialist should challenge complex guarantees, trust ownership, policy loans, cross-border issues and any proposed replacement. Schedule reviews after issue, after the first annual statement and whenever the household, ownership or financial need changes. Record who owns each review action.

faq.question: Is term insurance always better than whole life?
faq.answer: No. Term often fits large temporary needs efficiently; permanent coverage can fit durable needs. Suitability depends on guarantees, duration, affordability and alternatives.

faq.question: How much life insurance is enough?
faq.answer: Calculate immediate and ongoing survivor needs and goals, then subtract confirmed income and intended liquid assets. Use scenarios rather than a salary multiple.

faq.question: Is cash value guaranteed?
faq.answer: Some values may be guaranteed and others depend on dividends, crediting or investments. Read the contract and illustration columns separately.

faq.question: Can I borrow from a permanent policy tax free?
faq.answer: Loans have interest, reduce accessible value and benefits, and can create tax consequences if the policy lapses. Obtain jurisdiction-specific advice.

faq.question: Should children be named directly as beneficiaries?
faq.answer: Large direct payments to minors can create legal and control problems. Coordinate trusts, custodial rules and guardianship with qualified legal advice.

faq.question: When can an old policy be cancelled?
faq.answer: Only after replacement is issued, reviewed, accepted and effective, and after lost rights, new periods and costs are understood.

faq.question: How often should coverage be reviewed?
faq.answer: Review annually and after births, divorce, job changes, debt changes, business obligations, trust changes, relocation or retirement.

glossary.definition: The amount payable under policy terms after the insured person’s covered death.
Coverage designed for a specified period, usually without cash value.
Permanent coverage with contractually defined premiums, benefits and values, plus possible nonguaranteed dividends.
Permanent coverage with flexible elements whose guarantees and funding mechanics vary by design.
Policy value available under contract through surrender, withdrawal or loan, subject to conditions.
A presentation of guaranteed and nonguaranteed policy values under stated assumptions.
A contractual option to exchange eligible term coverage for specified permanent coverage without new evidence of insurability.
An amendment adding, limiting or changing policy coverage.
The recipient designated if the primary beneficiary cannot receive the proceeds.
An updated projection showing how an existing policy may perform under current values and assumptions.
